Rap Session
RAP SESH-un
noun (Boomer slang)
From rap, to talk freely and at length, African-American slang of the 1960s (perhaps from the older rap, to utter sharply or suddenly — Webster 1828 gives "to utter with sudden violence"), + session. Rap session, an open, informal group discussion, appears in the late 1960s and was everywhere in the early 1970s: campus dorms, church youth groups, encounter groups, and the consciousness-raising circles of the women’s movement. Rap as a music genre came later (late 1970s).

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

A rap session was a 1970s group conversation: everyone sitting in a circle, talking openly about feelings, problems, politics, or faith, with no set agenda. Youth groups had them; therapy groups ran on them; churches tried them. The Christian observation: the rap session reached for something Scripture commends — honest talk among friends — and also illustrates something Scripture warns about. The commendation: "Iron sharpeneth iron; so a man sharpeneth the countenance of his friend" (Pro 27:17). "Without counsel purposes are disappointed: but in the multitude of counsellors they are established" (Pro 15:22). And in Malachi’s day, "they that feared the LORD spake often one to another: and the LORD hearkened, and heard it, and a book of remembrance was written before him" (Mal 3:16) — God Himself listened in on that rap session. The warning: talk is not the same as wisdom, and much talk is often the opposite. "In the multitude of words there wanteth not sin: but he that refraineth his lips is wise" (Pro 10:19). Many 1970s rap sessions became exercises in sharing feelings with no anchor — every opinion equal, no one in charge, no Word on the table. That is the folly of Pro 18:2: "A fool hath no delight in understanding, but that his heart may discover itself." The best Christian rap session has an open Bible in the middle of the circle, a mature believer guiding it, and the rule of James: "swift to hear, slow to speak" (Jas 1:19).

Webster 1828 Definition

Late-1960s–70s slang (from AAVE rap, to talk freely) for an open, informal group discussion — honest talk Scripture commends when it sharpens (Pro 27:17) and warns against when it is many words without the Word (Pro 10:19).

RAP SESSION, n. (Boomer slang, late 1960s–70s) An informal, open group discussion, especially one for airing personal problems or views. From rap (v., 1960s AAVE), to talk freely, to converse.

Webster (1828) — RAP, verb transitive To strike with a quick blow; to knock. with one great peal they rap the door. To rap out, to utter with sudden violence; as, to rap out an oath. [In the popular language of the United States, it is often pronounced rip, to rip out an oath; Latin crepo.]

Decode for families: the youth-group "rap session" of 1972 is the "small group" of 2022. The question is the same: is there a Bible in the circle?

Pro 27:17 — "Iron sharpeneth iron; so a man sharpeneth the countenance of his friend."

Pro 15:22 — "Without counsel purposes are disappointed: but in the multitude of counsellors they are established."

Mal 3:16 — "Then they that feared the LORD spake often one to another: and the LORD hearkened, and heard it, and a book of remembrance was written before him for them that feared the LORD, and that thought upon his name."

Pro 10:19 — "In the multitude of words there wanteth not sin: but he that refraineth his lips is wise."

Jas 1:19 — "Wherefore, my beloved brethren, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath:"

Modern Corruption

The rap session sought honest community through open talk but often made feelings the authority and words the goal; Scripture commends counsel among the godly and warns that in the multitude of words there wanteth not sin.

expand to see more

The rap session was the liturgy of the therapeutic 1970s. Its unspoken creed was that talking about a problem is solving it, that every feeling deserves expression, and that no one in the circle may judge anyone else. Some good came of it — people who had never spoken honestly found that they could. But much of it was talk without truth. Proverbs warns that the fool’s delight is not understanding but self-display (Pro 18:2), and a circle where everyone discovers his heart and no one hears God’s Word is a circle of fools, however kind.

The church’s version is older and better. Malachi’s faithful remnant spoke often to one another, and the LORD listened (Mal 3:16). Their talk was anchored in the fear of the LORD. A family or a youth group that talks honestly around the Scriptures, with elders guiding and the young swift to hear, has the real thing.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Middle English rappen (to strike) → rap (to utter sharply; 1828) → 1960s AAVE rap (to talk freely) + session → late-1960s rap session.

expand to see more

Middle English rappen — to strike, to knock (imitative)

Rap — to utter suddenly or sharply; to rap out an oath (1828)

1960s AAVE: rap — to talk, to converse freely

Late 1960s–70s: rap session — open group discussion; consciousness-raising groups

Late 1970s: rap as a music genre (a later, separate development)
